location: Sec. 5.2 (class definitions); Table 3 'Class' column; Table 6; Figure 4 D4
problem: The five identifiability classes, which are contribution (ii), do not form a classification. They mix three different axes: which observation is needed (I-a, I-b), why the pair is confounded (I-c, I-d) and what the literature shows (I-e). They are not mutually exclusive, and apart from CuC none is derived from the formal definition given in Sec. 5.2.
evidence: Table 3 needs hybrid labels ('I-b / I-c', 'I-c / I-e', 'I-a / I-b'). Every I-b pair becomes I-d once the added observation is missing (I-b lists 'plan, host side information, external evidence' while I-d is 'missing ... side information'). I-e records an epistemic state, while I-a to I-d are claimed properties of the physics. The Sec. 5.2 definition only requires that distributions are not exactly identical, so with continuous nuisances almost every pair is 'distinguishable' and no separation margin is defined. Only CuC is worked through (Sec. 5.3); the other 11 rows are asserted.
action_taken: Replaced the five-class scheme with two orthogonal axes (A: minimal observation set A0/A1-P,X,Q,H,G/A2/A-empty; B: dominant confounder B-N/B-P/B-I) plus a separate evidence status; distinguishability redefined with a total-variation margin at record length N (Eq. 9); Table 3, Table 6, Figure 4, Appendix D and MOE CSV rebuilt. Explicit derivations given for CuC, cancellation, cyclic, cross-pol and IM rows; other rows rest on stated assumptions.

location: Sec. 1.3; Sec. 3.4; Sec. 9.4 (novelty positioning)
problem: The novelty narrative is over-claimed. The 'entry-plane' dimension is the classical end-to-end link-budget decomposition. The mechanism-observable and distinguishability matrices duplicate the fault-signature and isolability matrices of the model-based fault-diagnosis (FDI) literature. Neither precedent is acknowledged.
evidence: Satellite textbooks (e.g., Maral & Bousquet, 'Satellite Communications Systems'; Pratt & Bostian) and ITU-R S.741 [12] already split total C/(N+I) into uplink C/N, uplink C/I (ASI, cross-pol), C/IM (payload), downlink C/N and downlink C/I. Those are the same planes as EP-U1/EP-P/EP-D. The FDI literature (Basseville & Nikiforov 1993; Gertler; Frisk/Krysander structural isolability) formalizes 'distinguishable under an observation operator over nuisance parameters'. Sec. 9.4 lists ITU-R and DVB-S2X precedents but presents the plane decomposition and the identifiability scheme as the integrative contribution. Confidence high.
action_taken: Sec. 1.3, 3.4 and 9.4 now acknowledge link-budget decomposition [N038; N006; N007] and model-based fault diagnosis (fault signatures, isolability) [N036; N037]; contribution narrowed to mapping these onto GEO ground-monitor observability with evidence grades; two concrete decision-changing cases added (downlink ASI invisible at large monitor; station-specific vs common cross-pol leakage). N036-N038 added from domain knowledge and not verified in this audit.

location: Sec. 5.3 Eq. (9) and following text; Table 3 row 'CuC vs. clean' ('Not at high C/I'); Sec. 9.2 S3
problem: The 0.043 dB argument confuses how large an effect is with whether it is identifiable. Estimator variance can resolve 0.043 dB. What actually blocks detection is nuisance uncertainty in host level and monitor calibration. With identical spectral shapes and a free host-level nuisance, CuC is exactly non-identifiable from the PSD at any C/I, so the qualifier 'at high C/I' is wrong.
evidence: The per-bin periodogram standard deviation is about 4.34/sqrt(K) dB. Averaging over K looks and M in-band bins gives about 4.34/sqrt(KM) dB, so KM of about 1e4 resolves 0.043 dB at 1 sigma. Under the Sec. 5.2 definition, S_h(1+rho) is indistinguishable from a host whose power is scaled by (1+rho). Typical monitor level uncertainty (tenths of a dB to about 1 dB) is the operational bound.
action_taken: Sec. 5.3 rewritten: periodogram-variance argument (4.34/sqrt(KM) dB), non-identifiability under host-level nuisance at any C/I, detectability only when 10log10(1+rho) exceeds level uncertainty; SNR-wall analogue cited [N035]; Table 3 CuC row and S3 updated.

location: Eq. (2) and Eq. (4) (scalar kappa_u, kappa_d); Sec. 5.3 'Cross-polar leakage tests'; Table 3 row 'Uplink vs. downlink cross-pol coupling' (I-e); Fig. 3 O5
problem: The I-e assignment comes from the scalar-coupling simplification, not from the physics. Discriminators of uplink versus downlink coupling that follow from the model itself are ignored. The scalar kappa_u also cannot represent the most common operational cause, a misaligned terminal.
evidence: (1) An earth-station polarization misalignment leaks only that station's carrier(s), giving a per-carrier kappa. Satellite-antenna or downlink coupling leaks the whole opposite transponder at a common XPD, so the leakage pattern across carriers in a cross-pol plus plan observation separates them. (2) Downlink leakage is a copy of the opposite transponder's output, including its IM products, noise floor and OMUX shape, and is not truncated by the co-pol IMUX. With staggered co/cross frequency plans, uplink leakage straddles two co-pol IMUX passbands and shows their truncation. (3) Separate co- and cross-pol receivers impose different phi_LO on uplink leakage. Sec. 1.1 itself lists terminal installation errors as a leading cause.
action_taken: Eq. (2) now separates common uplink coupling kappa_u from station-specific leakage kappa_u,q; Sec. 4 and 5.3 add discriminators (leakage pattern across carriers, IMUX truncation, copied IM/noise floor, different down-converter LO); Table 3 adds station-specific vs common pair and assigns A1-X(+P) when one coupling dominates, A-empty only for comparable common-mode couplings.

location: Table 3 row 'Uplink vs. downlink ASI' (I-c / I-e)
problem: The class assignment contradicts both the paper's own definitions and the physics. The row lists 'antenna geometry' as a separating added observation, which by Sec. 5.2 makes the pair I-b.
evidence: Uplink ASI traverses the victim transponder. It is visible at every monitoring site and downlink beam of that transponder, is band-limited by the victim IMUX and carries the victim's LO translation. Downlink ASI depends on the monitoring antenna's sidelobe gain toward the neighbouring satellite and changes with a second station or a small repointing. The 'weak payload signature at high back-off' caveat only removes the payload cue, not the geometry cue.
action_taken: Uplink vs downlink ASI reclassified A1-G (second site, repointing, antenna geometry) with B-P only at a single fixed site and high back-off; Table 6 consistent.

location: Table 2 legend and the co-pol PSD column (rows: ASI uplink, ASI downlink, cross-pol uplink and downlink, overdrive, broadband); Sec. 9.2 S1; Abstract
problem: Detection and recognition are conflated. Table 2 marks the co-pol PSD as carrying 'primary evidence' (filled dot) for mechanisms that Table 3 and S3 say it cannot separate. A filled dot here means only that energy is detectable, not that the mechanism can be discriminated. S1 also calls closed-set classifiers 'closed-set detection'.
evidence: Co-pol PSD is a filled dot for 'Cross-pol, uplink coupling' and 'downlink coupling', while Table 3 says 'Cross-pol leakage vs. unauthorized carrier: From co-pol PSD: No' and S3 says co-pol PSD is insufficient. S1 reads 'predominantly binary or closed-set detection', but Sec. 7.1 describes [67]-[69] as classifiers.
action_taken: Table 2 legend redefined as discriminating power against Table 3 look-alikes; co-pol PSD re-rated (open circle) for unauthorized, ASI, cross-pol, IM, overdrive, broadband; S1 reworded to 'binary detection or closed-set classification'.

location: Table 2 rows 'ASI, uplink entry' and 'ASI, downlink entry'; Sec. 5.1
problem: The physics of ASI observability is mis-rated. Uplink ASI is commonly co-frequency with occupied victim carriers, because neighbours reuse the same band plan and off-axis VSAT emissions overlay them. It then behaves like carrier-under-carrier, yet it gets a filled dot for co-pol PSD while CuC gets '–'. For downlink ASI, a large monitoring antenna (S.465/S.580-class sidelobes) strongly rejects the neighbour's downlink. The monitor may therefore not see the ASI that small customer terminals suffer, and Sec. 5.1 never states this observability limit.
evidence: Table 2: CuC co-pol PSD '–' but ASI-uplink co-pol PSD filled dot. Sec. 5.1 discusses receiver capabilities but not monitor-antenna versus user-terminal antenna discrimination. Confidence high.
action_taken: Sec. 4 states uplink ASI is often co-frequency (CuC-like); Table 2 ASI PSD rated conditional; Sec. 4/5.1 add monitor-antenna discrimination limit (downlink ASI at customer sites may be unobservable at monitor) with S.465 pattern reference [N039].

location: Sec. 6.1, first paragraph
problem: Calling CA-CFAR 'the standard tool for unexpected spectral peaks' in ground monitoring is unsupported. It rests on a 1968 radar paper [49] and contradicts Sec. 1.1, which describes operator practice as comparison against expected levels and spectral masks.
evidence: [49] Finn & Johnson (RCA Review 1968) concerns radar clutter. Sec. 1.1: 'carriers are compared with expected power levels and spectral masks, alarms fire on deviations' [2], [6]. No satellite-monitoring source is given for CA-CFAR.

location: Sec. 7.1 last sentence; Sec. 7.2 ('usual building blocks for plan-conditioned models [83]-[85]'); Sec. 7.4 (decision 'D-4', clean-only 5% alarm); Sec. 10.2; Table 6 ('receiver-consistent plan-error'); Sec. 1.3 ('referred to only ... Section 10.3')
problem: The companion programme's Stage B design leaks into the review's gap definition and its 'requirements'. The headline gap is the conjunction of exactly the programme's design features (mechanism classes, controlled payload, cross-pol, plan conditioning, unknown rejection), which is trivially unfilled. Programme-specific protocol rules and jargon are presented as review-derived requirements, contrary to the claim in Sec. 1.3.

'Plan-conditioned models' do not exist in the reviewed literature, so [83]-[85] cannot be their 'usual building blocks'. location: Sec. 3.4 taxonomy list; Table 1; Sec. 4 'Benign structures'
problem: The 'payload-aware' taxonomy omits well-known payload and receiver mechanisms and a classic benign look-alike.
evidence: (a) Passive intermodulation (PIM): multicarrier Tx power in OMUX, waveguide or shared Tx/Rx antenna hardware generates odd-order products that can fall into the receive band and are then processed as uplink-entry energy. This is a recognized GEO payload problem. (b) Nonlinearity of the satellite wideband receiver (LNA/down-converter) before the IMUX: a strong uplink can couple many transponders, a different plane from the per-channel TWTA. (c) Sun-outage (solar conjunction) noise rise at the monitor: a predictable benign look-alike of broadband interference. Confidence high for (a) and (c), medium-high for (b).
action_taken: PIM and wideband-receiver nonlinearity added to Table 1, Fig. 2 and MOE CSV; sun transit added to benign look-alikes and Table 3. These are E1 physical inferences; primary PIM/receiver-nonlinearity literature was not searched (budget).

location: Notation table (phi_LO 'common to a transponder'); Eq. (2); Sec. 3.4 EP-P bullet; Figure 2 (phi_LO drawn in the EP-U1 band)
problem: Three inconsistent placements are given for the satellite LO phase noise: pre-IMUX in Eq. (2), inside EP-P 'IMUX -> amplifier -> OMUX' in Sec. 3.4, and in EP-U1 in Figure 2. In addition, the converter is normally shared by every channel behind one wideband receiver, not 'a transponder'.
evidence: Eq. (2) multiplies the composite by exp(j phi_LO) before h_IMUX, which is physically correct for the receiver down-converter. Sec. 3.4 lists 'frequency-converter phase noise' under EP-P. Figure 2 writes 'satellite LO phase noise' under EP-U1. Separate co- and cross-pol receivers give different phi_LO, which matters for the correlation test in Sec. 5.3.
action_taken: phi_LO defined as the satellite receiver down-converter phase noise, per polarization receiver (phi_LO,co / phi_LO,x), placed in EP-P before the IMUX consistently in Eq. (2), Sec. 3.4, notation and Fig. 2; effect on co/cross correlation noted in Sec. 5.3.

location: Eq. (4) and following definition of kappa_d; Table 1 'Cross-polar coupling (downlink)'
problem: kappa_d lumps satellite transmit isolation and downlink depolarization together with the monitoring antenna's own cross-pol isolation. The last term is a site-specific monitoring artefact that customers do not experience. A diagnosis framework must separate it, for example by feed rotation or a second station.
evidence: 'kappa_d lumps satellite transmit-antenna isolation, downlink depolarization and monitoring-antenna isolation'. Monitor-feed isolation belongs with EP-R calibration state.
action_taken: kappa_d now covers satellite transmit isolation and downlink depolarization only; monitor-feed leakage kappa_R assigned to EP-R inside R{.}; Table 3 adds 'monitor-feed leakage vs true cross-pol interference'.

location: Sec. 7.4, text after Eq. (16)
problem: FPR@95TPR is wrongly called 'threshold-free'. It is a single operating point at an oracle threshold derived from test data; AUROC is the threshold-free summary. Three related gaps: the near-family pooled variant does not say whether families are sample-weighted or macro-averaged; D_U denotes both all unknowns (Eq. 15) and the near-family pool; and readers are not warned that unknown-positive FPR@95TPR is not numerically comparable with the ID-positive FPR95 of [91], [92].
evidence: 'FPR@95TPR is a descriptive threshold-free summary'. Eq. (16) fixes t_95 from test unknowns. The ID-positive FPR95 measures the fraction of OOD accepted, while this convention measures the fraction of known samples rejected.
action_taken: Sec. 7.4: FPR@95TPR described as a single operating point at a test-oracle threshold (AUROC is threshold-free); D_unk^near defined with sample-weighted pooling and per-family reporting; non-comparability with ID-positive FPR95 stated.

location: Sec. 3.2, after Eq. (5)
problem: 'Saleh's paper also proposes frequency-dependent (quadrature) forms' conflates two distinct models. The quadrature (in-phase/quadrature) form is an alternative frequency-independent representation; the frequency-dependent model is a separate construction with frequency-varying coefficients and filter-nonlinearity-filter structure.
evidence: Saleh 1981 title: 'Frequency-independent and frequency-dependent nonlinear models of TWT amplifiers'. The quadrature coefficients (about 1.96/0.99/2.53/2.82) belong to the frequency-independent I/Q form. Confidence about 80%.
action_taken: Sec. 3.2 now: Saleh gives an equivalent I/Q form of the frequency-independent model and a separate frequency-dependent model.

location: Sec. 3.3, after Eq. (8) (ITU-R SM.1446 [22])
problem: The qualification of the 2 dB/dB slope rests on a secondary-only excerpt of a recommendation about transmitter IM measurement, not a satellite multicarrier TWT model. AM/PM-generated IM, which dominates TWTAs near saturation, is not mentioned.
evidence: [22] is tagged 'secondary record only', and the text admits 'search-excerpt level evidence'. Classic multicarrier TWT analyses (Shimbo, Proc. IEEE 1971; Fuenzalida et al. [23]) treat the AM/AM and AM/PM IM contributions directly.
action_taken: N010 (SM.1446) removed; near-saturation slope reduction supported by classical multicarrier TWT analyses [N032; R058] with explicit AM/PM contribution.

location: Sec. 3.3, end of second paragraph ([28])

action_taken: [R063] now cited for amplifier nonlinearity being identity-bearing, which motivates varying payload parameters as a design recommendation; invalid 'supports randomization' transfer removed.

The 'gain setting (operational cause)' of overdrive is an on-board command at EP-P, not EP-U0/EP-U1.

location: Table 3 rows 'Overdrive vs. broadband uplink interference' (I-c), 'Pulsed interference vs. TDMA traffic' (I-d), 'CuC vs. legitimate PCMA or CID' (I-d)
problem: These class assignments conflict with the paper's own definitions because each row lists an added observation that separates the pair (the definition of I-b).
evidence: Overdrive: the 'plan-referenced regrowth pattern' separates it, since IM3 regrowth extends to plan-predictable offsets beyond the carrier edges while noise-like uplink interference is flat across the IMUX passband. Pulsed vs. TDMA: TDMA bursts are RRC-shaped at planned frequencies, whereas radar pulses or chirps are not plan-aligned, and IQ modulation differs. CuC vs. CID: 'CID decoding' separates them.
action_taken: Handled by the RT-01 restructuring: overdrive vs broadband A1-P (B-P,B-I); pulsed vs TDMA A1-P/Q (B-I); CuC vs PCMA/CID A1-P or A2 (B-I).

location: Table 2 cells 'Payload IM (nominal) / Spectrogram' ('–') and 'Cross-pol, uplink coupling / Carrier plan' (hollow dot)
problem: Two ratings are physically questionable. IM products appear, disappear and change level coherently with carrier activation and TDMA bursts, so a spectrogram correlated with plan activity is a discriminating cue. The opposite-polarization plan predicts the frequency, bandwidth and symbol rate of a leaked carrier, which is primary evidence when no cross-pol receiver exists.

location: Sec. 5.3 'Host cancellation' (Eq. 11); Sec. 6.2; Sec. 6.3 ('no universal scaling law is asserted')
problem: The review misses the quantitative E1 content that would distinguish it from a conventional survey. It also omits the classic contrary result on residual-energy detection of weak signals, the noise-uncertainty SNR wall.
evidence: Residual host power from cancellation errors is about theta_rms^2 for phase error (1 deg rms gives about -35 dB) and epsilon^2 for amplitude error (0.1 dB gives about -39 dB). Detecting a C/I = 20 dB under-carrier therefore needs host suppression of at least 20 dB plus margin, so payload AM/PM, OMUX group delay and LO phase noise budgets directly set CuC detectability. Tandra & Sahai, 'SNR walls for signal detection' (IEEE JSTSP 2008) shows that energy detection of weak signals fails under noise-power uncertainty, which is directly relevant to Eq. (11) with I/N below 0 dB. Standard SCF detection-SNR scaling with record length under stated assumptions is also available.
action_taken: Sec. 5.3 adds E1 cancellation-depth derivation (eps^2+theta^2; 1 deg -> -35 dB; 0.1 dB -> -39 dB; >20 dB suppression for C/I=20 dB), SNR-wall reference [N035] and conditional SCF record-length scaling (N ~ rho_eff^-2 under a stated Gaussian-background model).
